profiles.name: Achillobator
profiles.summary: Achillobator, a large dromeosaurid theropod, is a nocturnal species, roaming the biomes of Gondwa and Riparia. Often accompanied by companion Latenivenatrix, Achillobator form strong pairbonds that often take entire lifetimes. Quiet, calm, and highly intelligent, these carnivores prefer to hunt larger targets with strong legs and sharp sickle talons.

analog.label: Caracal + Maned wolf
analog.headline: A night-hunting caracal that lives as a lifelong maned-wolf pair and hunts big game with its rook-like Latenivenatrix partners.

profiles.name: Albertaceratops
profiles.summary: Albertaceratops was a fascinating species that roamed North America during the Late Cretaceous period, around 76 million years ago. A member of the ceratopsid family, this herbivorous dinosaur is known for its distinctive frill and unique horn arrangement, which set it apart from its close relatives. With its robust build and specialized teeth, Albertaceratops was well-adapted for grazing on the lush vegetation of its environment, making it an intriguing subject for paleontologists studying dinosaur evolution and diversity!

analog.label: European badger + Wild boar
analog.headline: A badger sett in a ceratopsian body: sow-led, bold sentries, pushy at food, and as fierce as a wild-boar sow once cubs are around.

profiles.name: Alioramus
profiles.summary: Alioramus are nomadic carnivores that thrive through mixed sex packs, composing a maximum of 2 females, and up to 6 males. Females long for a lifelong female companion, while males maintain a fluid, dominance-based hierarchy within a pack. They travel long distances, and run down their prey to the point of exhaustion, nipping at them frequently to wear them down over time.

analog.label: African wild dog
analog.headline: An African wild dog pack: eight nomads that run prey to exhaustion with tag-team bites.

profiles.name: Allosaurus
profiles.summary: Allosaurus is a versatile, hardy theropod with a preference for arid environments, capable of surviving in these climates both in groups and alone due to their confidence in hunting a wide variety of prey. Being naturally tolerant to other species, Allosaurus find joy in following other creatures from a distance, observing their patterns and behaviours. Allosaurus travel long distances at night, and prefer to seek shelter in caves or underbrush during the brightest hours of the day.

analog.label: Asiatic lion + Bobcat
analog.headline: An Asiatic lion of the dry country, living in coalitions of two or three and hunting with a bobcat's night-time stealth.

profiles.name: Amargasaurus
profiles.summary: Amargasaurus is a docile species and happily integrates into other sauropod herds. Their wailing cries can be heard from almost every biome. Both genders have friendly depositions and show no jealousy, even during courtship. When preparing to lay eggs, Amargasaurus uniquely flush into bright colors, caused by an over indulgence of berries.

analog.label: Wildebeest + Giraffe
analog.headline: A chatty wildebeest in a giraffe's body, living in the shadow of the giant sauropods.

profiles.name: Anodontosaurus
profiles.summary: Anodontosaurus is an aloof, independent and stubborn dinosaur. While tolerant by nature, they are not inherently social and most favor a predominantly solitary lifestyle.

analog.label: Wombat + Honey badger
analog.headline: A stubborn wombat in tank armour with a honey badger's refusal to back down.

profiles.name: Apatosaurus
profiles.summary: Apatosaurus are massive, nomadic species defined by their strong family groupings - known as pods - led by an elder female known as the matriarch. Though generally calm and tolerant, they carry an underlying irritability, and are quick to assert themselves with overwhelming force if they feel their space or resources are threatened.

analog.label: African savanna elephant
analog.headline: An African elephant herd, scaled up to a sauropod.

profiles.name: Argentinosaurus
profiles.summary: Argentinosaurus is a genus of giant sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina. Although it is only known from fragmentary remains, Argentinosaurus is one of the largest known land animals of all time, perhaps the largest.

analog.label: Giraffe + Gorilla (silverback troop)
analog.headline: A gentle giant: a silverback's family life inside a giraffe's body, scaled up to the largest land animal ever.

profiles.name: Austroraptor
profiles.summary: Austroraptor is a semi-aquatic dromaeosaurid roaming the seaways and waterways of Riparia and Gondwa. Austroraptor rely heavily on their mated pair as a source of protection and connection, but may temporarily socialize with other adults in the same POI. Austroraptor are primarily fishers, but enjoy taking advantage of their ability to firmly hold small prey, often toying with them before killing them.

analog.label: Grey heron + Emperor penguin
analog.headline: A heron that fishes and drowns small prey, living like a penguin: devoted pair, swims the seas, breeds in a crowded colony.

profiles.name: Barsboldia
profiles.summary: Barsboldia was a large, herbivorous hadrosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, around 70 million years ago, in what is now Mongolia. Known for its long, flat snout and possible crest, Barsboldia likely fed on a variety of plant materials. It was a member of the duck-billed dinosaurs, and like others in its group, it may have traveled in herds for protection from predators.

analog.label: Wild Bactrian camel + Desert elephant
analog.headline: A Gobi camel herd with an elephant mother's heart: a salt-hungry desert nomad that barely notices carnivores.

profiles.name: Camptosaurus
profiles.summary: Camptosaurus are territorial herbivores that live in a large group known as a colony. Despite living in close quarters with one another, Camptosaurus are solitary, maintaining a home range that borders others’. They rarely interact with other Camptosaurus outside of courtship, nesting, and defending their territory.

analog.label: Quokka + American pika
analog.headline: A quokka colony where every neighbour guards its own little patch like a pika.

profiles.name: Ceratosaurus
profiles.summary: Ceratosaurus was a medium-sized theropod dinosaur known for its distinctive horn on its nose, and crests over its eyes. It had a long tail, sharp teeth, and was likely a fast, agile predator. Fossils of Ceratosaurus have been found in North America, dating back to the Late Jurassic period.

analog.label: Grey wolf
analog.headline: A forest wolf pack that would rather steal a kill than make one.

profiles.name: Citipati
profiles.summary: Citipati was a bird-like dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period, around 75 million years ago, found in what is now Mongolia. Known for its distinctive crest and close relationship to modern birds, Citipati was an omnivore, likely feeding on plants, small animals, and eggs. Famous for its fossilized nesting behavior, Citipati would sit atop its eggs, much like modern birds. Its parental care and brooding instincts give us unique insights into the connection between dinosaurs and birds.

analog.label: Chicken (red junglefowl)
analog.headline: A barnyard flock gone wild: roosters with harems of hens, dawn crowing, broody hens stealing chicks.

profiles.name: Compsognathus
profiles.summary: Compsognathus is a tiny, meat-eating dinosaur that spends its time scurrying between POIs and scavenging from carcasses. About the size of a chicken, it is one of the smallest dinosaurs on the roster. Relying on its speed and agility to catch critters and for general defence, Compsognathus frequently follows and stalks other, larger predators for opportunities to feast on their kills. This is primarily seen with Tyrannosaurus, who look at Compsognathus fondly.

analog.label: Brown rat + Golden jackal
analog.headline: A swarm of rats with a jackal's knack for shadowing the big predators.

profiles.name: Concavenator
profiles.summary: Concavenators are swift, agile predators skilled in hunting on both land and water. As a social species they thrive in loosely bonded groups for selfish reasons and move between key areas on their endless hunts for sustenance. This medium carnivore is known for their trinket hoarding tendencies, as well as their brutal feeding habits, often ripping their prey apart in a matter of minutes.

analog.label: Giant otter + Stoat
analog.headline: A gang of giant otters, the 'river wolves' that kill crocodiles, with a stoat's ferocity and a hoarder's temper.

profiles.name: Daspletosaurus
profiles.summary: Daspletosaurus is a tyrannosaurid theropod dinosaur that roams Gondwa and Riparia in small packs, led by a dominant, bonded male pair. Females work together to raise offspring, and fiercely stand their ground in their defense.  These intelligent hunters work together to herd prey into dead ends and corners, making easier kills. Daspletosaurus are confident and unstoppable, working together to best their opponents and prey.

analog.label: Dingo + Cougar
analog.headline: A dingo pack led by dominant males that herds prey into dead ends, with a cougar's forest-and-cliff ambush.

profiles.name: Deinocheirus
profiles.summary: Deinocheirus was a bizarre, large theropod dinosaur that lived around 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Mongolia. It had an unusual combination of features, including massive arms with large claws, a long snout, and a humped back. Despite its fearsome appearance, Deinocheirus was an omnivore, feeding on plants, fish, and small animals. It could grow up to 35 feet long, making it one of the largest members of its group, and its strange, mixed diet and anatomy have puzzled paleontologists since its discovery.

analog.label: Mute swan + Moose
analog.headline: A lifelong swan pair in a moose's body: a gentle lake giant and fierce parent that splashes predators away.

profiles.name: Deinonychus
profiles.summary: Deinonychus are extremely aggressive , social and noisy small carnivores that live in groups called a dynasty when females are present - or troops when a group consists of all males. Dynasties are lead by a female - the Mother to all other females in the group - and experience a high level of behavioral dimorphism between the sexes. Males are low ranking, submissive, and expected to keep in line with hyper aggressive females, who fight and squabble amongst each other to gain favor with the Mother.

analog.label: Spotted hyena + Dwarf mongoose
analog.headline: A spotted-hyena clan shrunk to mongoose size: noisy, female-ruled and deadly in numbers.

profiles.name: Deinosuchus
profiles.summary: Deinosuchus was a massive prehistoric crocodile that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, around 80 to 73 million years ago. Growing up to 33 feet long, it was one of the largest crocodyliforms to ever exist. Deinosuchus lived in rivers and coastal environments, preying on dinosaurs and other large animals that ventured near the water’s edge. With its powerful jaws and ambush tactics, it was a dominant predator, capable of taking down prey as large as a hadrosaur.

analog.label: Nile crocodile
analog.headline: A Nile crocodile with sea legs: lazy basker, ambush at the water's edge, death rolls.

profiles.name: Dilophosaurus
profiles.summary: Dilophosaurus was a fast, agile predator that lived during the Early Jurassic period, around 193 million years ago. Recognizable by the two crests on its head, this dinosaur measured about 20 feet long. Likely hunting small to medium-sized prey, Dilophosaurus used its speed and sharp teeth to catch food. Its crests may have been used for display during courtship or social interactions, making it a distinctive and striking figure in its ecosystem.

analog.label: Red fox + Raccoon
analog.headline: A cunning, skittish fox family that turns dangerous in a group, with a raccoon's sneakiness.

profiles.name: Dryosaurus
profiles.summary: Dryosaurus is a small, agile herbivorous dinosaur that travels across multiple POIs, laying claim to caves, perches and resources. Dryosaurus are highly territorial and band together to ward off other dinosaurs much larger or stronger than them.

analog.label: Wild rabbit + Baboon troop
analog.headline: A rabbit warren with a baboon troop's attitude and chihuahua energy.

profiles.name: Eotriceratops
profiles.summary: Eotriceratops is a social and migratory species, led by a female individual called the matriarch. With powerful memories and memorized migration paths, Eotriceratops females prioritize their matriarchies and the offspring within their herds. Eotriceratops males patrol their herds fiercely, erupting into aggressive battles for dominance with one another and against any predators or herbivores that threaten their herd and its resources. A male's innate aggression can, at times, even be turned towards their own offspring.

analog.label: Asian elephant + Hippopotamus (bull)
analog.headline: An Asian elephant matriarchy whose bulls carry a hippo bull's temper.

profiles.name: Eurhinosaurus
profiles.summary: Eurhinosaurus was a sleek, fast-swimming marine reptile that lived during the Early Jurassic period, around 180 million years ago, in what is now Europe. This remarkable ichthyosaur was known for its extremely elongated upper jaw, which extended far beyond its lower jaw like a swordfish’s bill. Reaching lengths of up to 6–7 meters, Eurhinosaurus was a powerful predator, using its long snout and numerous sharp teeth to catch small fish and squid. Its name, meaning "well-nosed lizard," highlights its distinctive jaw structure, and its streamlined body and large flippers made it an efficient, agile swimmer in the ancient seas.

analog.label: Bottlenose dolphin
analog.headline: A loud, playful dolphin pod with a swordfish bill that treats hunting as sport.

profiles.name: Giganotosaurus
profiles.summary: Giganotosaurus are nomadic apex predators. They are powerful and calculated and known for endurance-based hunting, able to run down prey over long distances. Giganotosaurus thrive in solitude or fragile, temporary bonds that only become permanent through proven nesting success.

analog.label: Jaguar
analog.headline: A lone jaguar the size of a tiger: water-loving, tree-marking, and ready to fight any other apex for the right to stay.

profiles.name: Halszkaraptor
profiles.summary: Halszkaraptor is a unique species of small, bird-like dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous period. Discovered in Mongolia, this dromaeosauridae had a distinctive combination of traits, including a long neck, webbed limbs, and a streamlined body, suggesting it was semi-aquatic. Its adaptations point to a lifestyle similar to modern water birds, making it one of the most unusual dinosaur discoveries. Halszkaraptor's features provide valuable insight into the diverse evolutionary paths taken by dinosaurs. It was about the size of the common Mallard Duck!

analog.label: Mallard + Magpie
analog.headline: A raft of mallards that mobs anything near the nest, with a magpie's eye for shiny things.

profiles.name: Hatzegopteryx
profiles.summary: Hatzegopteryx is a large pterosaur that are fiercely protective - yet deeply affectionate - towards their chosen mates and offspring. After completing spectacular aerial dives at their universal courtship grounds, Hatzegopteryx pair for life, and head out to find and claim a territory to defend together. They specialize in hunting prey they can carry, and dropping them from a height.

analog.label: Golden eagle
analog.headline: A pair of golden eagles holding a huge territory, grabbing prey and dropping it from the sky.

profiles.name: Iguanodon
profiles.summary: Iguanodons are hot-headed and aggressive herbivores. They are highly social and roam in herds, forming tight bonds with certain individuals within their groupings. These large herbivores are known for their stubborn dispositions and picky personalities, often turning their ire on those not within their herd.

analog.label: Cape buffalo
analog.headline: A Cape buffalo herd: bulls in front, three defenders who chase predators down, and stubborn about every bush and puddle.

profiles.name: Kaiwhekea
profiles.summary: Kaiwhekea is an extinct genus of plesiosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian age) of what is now New Zealand. Kaiwhekea belongs to the clade Aristonectinae inside the family Elasmosauridae.

analog.label: Sea lion + Sea turtle
analog.headline: A sea-lion colony in a long-necked, turtle-like body: basks on beaches, plays in the surf, hunts in turns.

profiles.name: Kelenken
profiles.summary: Kelenken was a large "terror bird" that lived approximately 15 million years ago in what we now call Argentina. "Terror” bird is an apt description of Kelenken, who was flightless and possessed a strong and heavy body, equipped with a powerful ripping beak. Kelenken was thought to have reached heights of up to 3m, and weighed in at over 220lbs.

analog.label: Secretary bird
analog.headline: A pack of secretary birds: long-legged ground hunters that run prey down and stomp it.

profiles.name: Kentrosaurus
profiles.summary: Kentrosaurus was a small, herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic period. It belonged to the stegosaur family, known for its distinctive row of bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail. It likely used its tail spikes for defense against predators. This dinosaur primarily lived in what is now Africa and fed on low-lying plants and vegetation.

analog.label: Llama + Porcupine
analog.headline: A spitting llama guard with porcupine spikes, the sentry of the stegosaur herd.

profiles.name: Lambeosaurus
profiles.summary: Lambeosaurus are a social and gregarious herd species who travel closely along waterways that they use to their advantage when fleeing from predators. Lambeosaurus herds move away from predators as one unit, synchronizing their motions to make it confusing for predators and to defend their herd members. Lambeosaurus does are more dominant and initiate courtship, while Lambeosaurus bucks are more submissive. Parents work closely together to raise their fragile fawns.

analog.label: Sambar deer + Sheep (flock)
analog.headline: A river-hugging sambar deer herd that moves like one flock of sheep.

profiles.name: Latenivenatrix
profiles.summary: Latenivenatrix, a large troodontid, form large, social, and noisy rookeries. Latenivenatrix is often observed singing, dancing, jumping, and playing with other Latenivenatrix. Uniquely, Latenivenatrix may also form bonds with Achillobator, whom act as hunting partners and strong allies.

analog.label: Rook + Dhole
analog.headline: A noisy rook colony that hunts at night like a dhole pack and rides along on Achillobator hunts.

profiles.name: Leedsichthys
profiles.summary: Leedsichthys are massive filter-feeding pachycormid fish that live in the oceans of Riparia. Solitary in nature when adult, Leedsichthys fathers raise their offspring in massive batches, migrating alongside them and protecting them. Females, on the other hand, migrate on their own, temporarily forming bonds with others they come across in their travels.

classification.label: Apex Cathemeral Aquatic Filter Feeder Carnivore

analog.label: Whale shark + Bowfin
analog.headline: A gentle whale shark on an endless migration loop, where the fathers raise the young.

profiles.name: Lurdusaurus
profiles.summary: Lurdusaurus originated from the Elrhaz Formation in Niger, found in the Cretaceous period around 112 million years ago. It was an iguanodont that may have been semi-aquatic, living in and around the rivers of ancient tropical forests. Measuring eight meters long (26 feet) and weighing more than five tons, Lurdusaurus were formidable herbivores with a diet consisting primarily of water-plants.

analog.label: Hippopotamus + Capybara
analog.headline: A medium-sized hippo pod: water by day, land at night, and a dominant bull who owns the river.

profiles.name: Maip
profiles.summary: Maip is a genus of large megaraptorid hailing from Late Cretaceous Argentina, described from an incomplete and disarticulated skeleton. Among other megaraptorians, Maip is considered the largest on record. Their behavior resembles that of both hyenas and corvids; intelligent and very sociable animals, Maip take on the role of endurance hunter, bleeding down their prey with sharpened claws and swift movement.

analog.label: Spotted hyena + Common raven
analog.headline: A bone-crunching, night-shrieking hyena pair with a raven's cruel intelligence.

profiles.name: Megalania
profiles.summary: Megalania is a medium cathemeral predator that inhabits many different types of terrain across Gondwa. Split into two specific variants - arid & temperate - this species has different populations, reflected in different colors and patterns. Both variants are highly aggressive to one another. These predators are solitary, but may tolerate some company - though this varies between individuals, and variants.

analog.label: Komodo dragon + Nile monitor
analog.headline: A Komodo dragon in the dry country and a Nile monitor in the wetlands: two rival variants of one solitary scavenger-hunter.

profiles.name: Metriacanthosaurus
profiles.summary: Metriacanthosaurus roamed during the Late Jurassic period and had a preference for coastal environments. Their striking, vibrant coloration aids in courting and serves as a warning to any potential predators who roam Riparia and Gondwa. With poisonous scales covering their entire body, making a meal of this nocturnal carnivore is a risk which may not be worth taking.

analog.label: Gila monster + Poison dart frog
analog.headline: A poisonous, neon-bright night hunter: a Gila monster's lifestyle with a poison dart frog's toxins and turf wars.

profiles.name: Pachycephalosaurus
profiles.summary: Pachycephalosaurus are small terrestrial herbivores that thrive on the mountainous regions of Gondwa. Congregating in large groups, females socialize in personality specific hierarchies while males challenge for rights to all the females. Though confident when faced with danger, Pachycephalosaurus are inherently flighty on open terrain and retreat to perched rocks, cliffs and caves when threatened.

analog.label: Mountain goat + Bighorn sheep
analog.headline: A mountain goat band on the cliffs, with bighorn rams' head-butting duels.

profiles.name: Pachyrhinosaurus
profiles.summary: Pachyrhinosaurus are large, relatively docile ceratopsians that group with other, similar species, and migrate over long distances throughout Gondwa in search of food. Led by an elder female, males form defensive bands known as shields, consisting of related males that work together to protect the whole group - known as a migration.

analog.label: Musk ox + Caribou / reindeer
analog.headline: A musk ox wall on a caribou-style migration, led by the eldest cow.

profiles.name: Parasaurolophus
profiles.summary: Parasaurolophus are large, adaptable herbivores known for their deep, resonant calls amplified by their iconic crests. They live in tight-knit herds, relying on vocal communication while they migrate over vast distances. Calm but vigilant, they migrate between seasonal feeding grounds, balancing safety in numbers with cautious curiosity.

analog.label: Red deer + Przewalski's horse
analog.headline: A red-deer herd with a head stag and his does, migrating along ancestral routes like wild horses.

profiles.name: Psittacosaurus
profiles.summary: Psittacosaurus are small, social ceratopsians that survive through cooperation, vigilance, and clever evasion rather than brute strength. They live in groups known as passels, led by a sole elderly individual known as the Quillguard, who is responsible for maintaining order within a group. A keen sentry species, Psittacosaurus are readily welcomed into ceratopsian herds.

analog.label: Meerkat + Virginia opossum
analog.headline: A meerkat mob of sentries led by an elder, surviving through vigilance and an opossum's clever evasion.

profiles.name: Pycnonemosaurus
profiles.summary: Pycnonemosaurus are large, carnivorous dinosaurs that travel endlessly across Gondwa in search of prey - or simply entertainment. Often referred to as clownish, they enjoy following and chasing various species. Brutish, these carnivores often shove and push at each other, but seem to mutually enjoy this type of roughhousing.

analog.label: Wild boar + Lion
analog.headline: A rowdy wild-boar gang with a lion's habit of killing rival predators.

profiles.name: Quetzalcoatlus
profiles.summary: Quetzalcoatlus is a large, intimidating pterosaur that is found across the entirety of Gondwa. They are often seen following migrating herds and predators, feeding from corpses at common dying grounds, and bullying other carnivores off of their corpses. Forming small, loosely bonded groups, Quetzalcoatlus are widely known as lazy scavengers, and typically poor parents.

analog.label: Vulture + Marabou stork
analog.headline: A committee of vultures that walks the ground like a marabou stork and bullies hunters off their kills.

profiles.name: Rhamphorhynchus
profiles.summary: Rhamphorhynchus are small aerial fishers and scavengers who form mutualistic relationships with sauropods such as Amargasaurus, Ampelosaurus, Apatosaurus and Argentinosaurus. They clean them of parasites while utilizing them as roosts for their flightless offspring. They are social within their colonies and form quick bonds with one another.

analog.label: Oxpecker + Parakeet
analog.headline: An oxpecker riding the sauropods, living in a noisy parakeet colony that copies every sound.

profiles.name: Sarcosuchus
profiles.summary: Sarcosuchus was an enormous prehistoric crocodile-like reptile that lived about 110 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous period. It could grow up to 40 feet in length and weighed around 8 tons, making it one of the largest crocodilians to have ever lived. Sarcosuchus primarily inhabited river systems in what is now Africa and likely preyed on creatures and large fish.

analog.label: Mugger crocodile + Jacana
analog.headline: A nomadic marsh crocodile trio run jacana-style by one fierce female, walking overland at night to hunt.

profiles.name: Spinosaurus
profiles.summary: Spinosaurus is a formidable semi-aquatic apex predator. Adorned with sharp claws, a thick paddle-like tail and tall sail along its back, this iconic predator is well known for dominating riverways. Selfish and territorial by nature, Spinosaurus in water see all invaders as competition over their resources and readily push out other species from their claimed water source.

analog.label: Grizzly bear + Saltwater crocodile
analog.headline: A grizzly that owns its stretch of river and fights like a saltwater crocodile, then relaxes with its rivals at the great falls.

profiles.name: Stegosaurus
profiles.summary: Stegosaurus is one of the only truly territorial species that mix herds with others of similar genus. Armed with spiked tails and a selfish attitude, they roam between resource rich areas and claim ownership of any food and water within their immediate vicinity. Known for their aggressive instincts, they are a force to be reckoned with - especially when smaller stegosaurids are nearby.

analog.label: Black rhinoceros + Grévy's zebra
analog.headline: A grumpy black rhino with a zebra stallion's family: one bull, three cows, and every bush within 10 body lengths is his.

profiles.name: Struthiomimus
profiles.summary: Struthiomimus was a fast, ostrich-like dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, around 75 million years ago, in North America. Standing up to 12 feet long, it had long legs built for running and a beak without teeth, likely feeding on a mix of plants and small animals. Its speed and agility helped it evade predators, making it one of the swiftest dinosaurs of its time. Struthiomimus was a nimble and social creature, possibly living in groups for protection.

analog.label: Ostrich
analog.headline: An ostrich flock: harems of hens, incredible running endurance, powerful kicks and the best eyes in the herd.

profiles.name: Styracosaurus
profiles.summary: Styracosaurus was a striking ceratopsian dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period, around 75 million years ago, in what is now North America. Known for its large frill adorned with long, spiked horns and a prominent nose horn, Styracosaurus was both a defensive and visually impressive herbivore. Growing up to 18 feet long, it traveled in herds, grazing on low-lying vegetation. Its formidable appearance likely helped deter predators and played a role in social interactions within its group.

analog.label: Musk ox + Gemsbok (oryx)
analog.headline: The 'attack dog' of the ceratopsian herd: a musk-ox wall with oryx-style hit-and-run chargers.

profiles.name: Suchomimus
profiles.summary: Suchomimus are cunning and opportunistic semi-aquatic carnivores. Though usually tolerant, they are highly calculated, and always on the lookout for an easy advantage. These nomadic predators drift between resource-rich lakes and rivers, assessing every situation for personal gain. While not inherently aggressive, they fiercely guard any perceived benefit - usually a nearby Spinosaurus, which they treat as both a protector and provider. Though social in small groups, Suchomimus are largely indifferent to others of their kind, and prefer intimidation and vocal threats over direct conflict.

analog.label: Gharial + Coyote
analog.headline: A fish-snatching gharial with a coyote's calculating mind, and a cuckoo's trick for getting Spinosaurus to raise its young.

profiles.name: Tenontosaurus
profiles.summary: Tenontosaurus was a medium-sized herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 115 million years ago, in what is now North America. Growing up to 23 feet long, it had a long, sturdy tail used for balance and possibly defense. Tenontosaurus fed on low-lying vegetation and likely moved in herds for protection from predators like Deinonychus. Its mix of size, agility, and powerful tail made it a resilient herbivore in its environment.

analog.label: White-lipped peccary + Common marmoset
analog.headline: A peccary herd sharing one scent and fighting as a team, run marmoset-style by one matriarch with doting fathers.

profiles.name: Thalassodromeus
profiles.summary: Thalassodromeus was a large pterosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 110 million years ago in what is now Brazil. Known for its enormous head crest, which could be as long as its entire skull, Thalassodromeus likely used this feature for display and possibly thermoregulation. With a wingspan of around 15 feet, it was a strong flyer, likely feeding on fish and other small prey along ancient coastlines. Its name, meaning "sea runner," reflects its close association with marine environments.

analog.label: Pigeon + Black-headed gull
analog.headline: A huge, chatty pigeon flock of the inland rivers that eats like a gull: fish, stolen scraps and messy dive-bombing.

profiles.name: Therizinosaurus
profiles.summary: Therizinosaurus are a nocturnal species of herbivore, forming groups of related females and unrelated males, with one dominant female called the Dame. Females, called hens, are aggressive and territorial, and males, called roosters, are paternal and conflict-avoidant. They spend most of their lives deep in the forests of Gondwa, preferring to avoid sharing their space with other species.

analog.label: Cassowary
analog.headline: A cassowary blown up to Apex size: dagger-clawed, forest-dwelling, ruled by aggressive females while the gentle males raise the chicks.

profiles.name: Torvosaurus
profiles.summary: Torvosaurus is a large theropod carnivore that forms large groups, known as packs. Led by a single male, the females are responsible for hunting and providing for the group, while males fend off rivals and keep the group's temporary POI safe.

analog.label: African lion
analog.headline: A lion pride: the females hunt by day, the male guards the pride and fights off takeovers, and neighbouring prides team up on giants.

profiles.name: Tropeognathus
profiles.summary: Tropeognathus originated from the Romualdo Formation in Brazil, dating back to the Early Cretaceous period around 112 million years ago. This large pterosaur had an impressive wingspan of up to 8.5 meters (28 feet) and is thought to have been a proficient flyer, inhabiting coastal regions and open seas. With its long, toothed jaws and distinctive keel-like crest, Tropeognathus specialized in a diet of fish, diving into the water to snatch prey with precision. Its lifestyle was likely social, with flocks congregating along shorelines or nesting in cliffs, much like modern seabirds.

analog.label: Herring gull + Great cormorant
analog.headline: A cheeky seagull colony that dives for fish like a cormorant and turns into a pack hunter at night.

profiles.name: Tylosaurus
profiles.summary: Tylosaurus are nomadic aquatic carnivores that form matrilineal groupings, with solitary and paired males being much more aggressive than internally peaceful matrilines. Matrilines may come together and form pods - larger groups of Tylosaurus that travel together and court. Tylosaurus are doting mothers, and protect their offspring fiercely.

analog.label: Orca
analog.headline: An orca matriline: the eldest mother leads, every family has its own hunting culture, and nothing in the sea is safe.

profiles.name: Tyrannosaurus
profiles.summary: Tyrannosaurus is a fearsome apex predator primarily found in forested areas. They are known for their territorial nature, and fiercely defend a territory from rival predators. These powerful carnivores are keen ambush hunters and seemingly blend into the environment unseen while waiting for the perfect opportunity to strike. With a jaw strength primed to take down large prey, Tyrannosaurus is a highly dangerous predator.

analog.label: Polar bear + Tawny owl
analog.headline: A polar bear's patience and power, living like a pair of tawny owls: mated for life, owning a forest, striking from cover.

profiles.name: Tyrannotitan
profiles.summary: Tyrannotitan are nocturnal apex predators known for their brutal aggression and hunting methods - often dousing themselves entirely in the blood of their prey or rivals. They keep to same sex related pairs, usually brothers, sisters, or a mother and daughter/father and son. They can often be heard before they are seen - broadcasting loud, haunting calls throughout the night in their search for prey.

analog.label: Tiger + Great white shark
analog.headline: A nocturnal tiger with a great white shark's bite: booming calls in the dark, then prey bleeding out behind it.

profiles.name: Utahraptor
profiles.summary: Utahraptor are highly social raptors that thrive in family groups. Known for their keen eyesight and pack coordination hunting strategy, Utahraptor are formidable predators of their size tier, capable of taking on a variety of prey.

analog.label: Grey wolf (family pack) + Bowerbird
analog.headline: A Yellowstone-style wolf family pack around an alpha pair, at war with rival packs, where suitors court with bowerbird gifts.

profiles.name: Yunnanosaurus
profiles.summary: Yunnanosaurus was a large sauropodomorph dinosaur from the late Triassic to the early Jurassic period - around 210 million years ago in what is now the Yunnan Province, in China. It reached up to 13 feet in length, is known for being one of the earliest sauropodomorphs, and is the dinosaur that gave rise to massive sauropods. Yunnanosaurus had a long neck and a small head, it was capable of both bipedal and quadrupedal movement.

analog.label: Moose + Red kangaroo
analog.headline: Calm and sociable in the dry season, furious as a rutting moose in the rain: it rears up like a boxing kangaroo, beats its chest and stomps small predators.

profiles.name: Yutyrannus
profiles.summary: Yutyrannus are a feathered tyrannosaurid who form either strongly bonded familial groupings, or loose groupings of unrelated individuals for socialization and courtship. Constantly singing, playing, and performing, Yutyrannus are incredibly showy, and enjoy building close bonds with the individuals around them. Yutyrannus prefer the cooler temperatures of the Rainy Season, and struggle to regulate their body temperatures in the Dry Season.

analog.label: Snow leopard + Arctic fox
analog.headline: A snow leopard that lives in a playful arctic-fox family: cold-loving, den-dwelling, and bold enough to hunt the biggest predators.
